subject: biology-hl
about: Original practice questions written for NevaIB from the IB guide's syllabus understandings and the school's unit order. Not IB past-paper questions, not publisher material and not IB markschemes: the marking points are written for self-marking. Organisms, experiments and data in data-response items are invented for practice.

items.stem: Which of these is NOT usually classed as an organelle?
choices: The cell wall
The mitochondrion
The nucleus
The Golgi apparatus
items.note: The cell wall, cytoskeleton and cytoplasm are not organelles: organelles are discrete structures within the cell with a specialised function. The wall is outside the membrane.

items.stem: Proteins that will be secreted from the cell are made by:
choices: Free ribosomes floating in the cytoplasm of the cell body
Ribosomes inside the nucleus next to the chromosomes
Ribosomes in the Golgi apparatus before packaging
Ribosomes attached to the rough endoplasmic reticulum
items.note: Bound ribosomes on rough ER make proteins for secretion, lysosomes and membranes; free ribosomes make proteins kept in the cytosol.

items.stem: The main role of the Golgi apparatus is to:
choices: Make proteins from amino acids according to the base sequence of each mRNA
Process and modify proteins and package them into vesicles for secretion
Release energy from glucose by aerobic respiration in its cisternae
Store the cell's genetic material and control its activities
items.note: The Golgi receives vesicles from the rough ER, modifies proteins (e.g. adds carbohydrate) and sends vesicles to the plasma membrane.

items.stem: One advantage of separating the nucleus from the cytoplasm is that:
choices: Transcription and translation can happen at the same time on one mRNA
Ribosomes can enter the nucleus easily and translate the DNA there directly
mRNA can be modified before translation, without ribosomes acting on it
The DNA is protected from all mutations caused by radiation
items.note: The nuclear membrane separates transcription from translation, so pre-mRNA can be processed (e.g. intron removal) first. In prokaryotes the two are coupled.

items.stem: Why does the nuclear membrane have pores?
choices: DNA must leave the nucleus so it can be copied in the cytoplasm
Ribosomes are assembled in the cytoplasm and must enter the nucleus to work
mRNA must leave the nucleus and proteins such as enzymes must enter
Pores let the nucleus divide without its membrane breaking down
items.note: Pores allow controlled exchange: mRNA and ribosome subunits out, proteins (e.g. DNA polymerase) in. DNA stays inside.

items.stem: Which feature of the mitochondrion is matched correctly to its function?
choices: The outer membrane contains ATP synthase that makes most ATP
The matrix holds chlorophyll that absorbs light for respiration
The intermembrane space contains the enzymes of the Krebs cycle
Cristae increase the surface area for the electron transport chain
items.note: Cristae (folded inner membrane) carry the ETC and ATP synthase; the matrix contains Krebs cycle enzymes; the small intermembrane space allows a steep proton gradient.

items.stem: In a chloroplast, the light-dependent reactions take place:
choices: In the stroma, which contains the Calvin cycle enzymes
On the thylakoid membranes, which hold the photosystems
In the outer envelope membrane, which faces the cytoplasm
In the starch grains, which store the products of the reactions
items.note: Thylakoid membranes (stacked into grana) give a large area for photosystems and ATP synthase; the stroma compartmentalises the Calvin cycle.

items.stem: Lysosomes keep their digestive enzymes inside a membrane. The main advantage is that:
choices: The enzymes cannot digest molecules in the cytoplasm of the cell
The enzymes can work at a higher temperature than the rest of the cytoplasm
The enzymes are made more quickly inside the lysosome
The enzymes are only needed when the cell is dividing
items.note: Compartmentalisation keeps harmful enzymes away from cell components and lets a different internal pH be maintained.

choices: Pumping protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane into the intermembrane space
Attaching free ribosomes to the membranes of the rough endoplasmic reticulum
Forming the protein-lined pores in the double membrane around the nucleus
Shaping the plasma membrane into a pit that pinches off as a vesicle
items.note: Clathrin proteins coat the membrane, curve it into a pit and help it bud off as a vesicle during endocytosis.

items.stem: During mitosis the nuclear membrane breaks into vesicles. The benefit is that:
choices: The DNA can be replicated in the cytoplasm
Ribosomes can translate DNA directly
The spindle can reach and move the chromosomes
The cell can absorb nutrients for growth
items.note: The spindle microtubules form in the cytoplasm; the membrane must break down so they can attach to centromeres. It re-forms around each new nucleus.

items.stem: A drug blocks movement of vesicles from the rough ER to the Golgi apparatus. Which process is affected most directly?
choices: Synthesis of haemoglobin by free ribosomes in a red blood cell precursor
Secretion of digestive enzymes by a pancreas cell
Production of ATP by aerobic respiration
Replication of DNA in the nucleus
items.note: Secreted proteins follow rough ER → vesicle → Golgi → vesicle → plasma membrane. Haemoglobin is made on free ribosomes and stays in the cell.

items.stem: Contrast the synthesis of proteins by free ribosomes with that by ribosomes bound to the rough endoplasmic reticulum.
markscheme: Free ribosomes make proteins for use in the cytoplasm / retained in the cell (1)
Bound ribosomes make proteins for secretion / for lysosomes / for membranes (1)
Proteins from bound ribosomes enter the ER lumen and are transported in vesicles; free ribosome proteins are released into the cytosol (1)
items.tactic: Contrast = differences only; always pair the two sides.

items.stem: Explain how the structure of a chloroplast is adapted to photosynthesis.
markscheme: Thylakoid membranes give a large surface area for photosystems / light absorption (1)
Small space inside thylakoids allows a steep proton gradient for ATP synthesis (1)
Stroma contains Calvin cycle enzymes, concentrated in one compartment (1)
Double membrane separates the reactions from the cytoplasm (1)
items.tactic: Pair each structure with how it helps — a list of structures without functions earns nothing.

items.stem: Describe the route taken by a protein that is made in a cell and then secreted.
markscheme: Made by ribosomes on the rough ER (1)
Enters the ER lumen and is carried in a vesicle to the Golgi apparatus (1)
Modified/processed in the Golgi (e.g. carbohydrate added) (1)
Packaged into vesicles that bud from the Golgi (1)
Vesicles fuse with the plasma membrane, releasing the protein by exocytosis (1)
items.tactic: Describe a pathway in order; name each organelle and the vesicle step between them.

items.stem:
(Invented data for practice.) In an invented experiment, cells were given radioactive amino acids for 3 minutes. The percentage of total radioactivity found in each compartment was measured: 3 min: rough ER 85%, Golgi 10%, secretory vesicles 5%; 20 min: rough ER 15%, Golgi 60%, vesicles 25%; 120 min: rough ER 5%, Golgi 10%, vesicles 85%.
(a) Describe the change in radioactivity in the Golgi apparatus. (b) Explain what the data show about the route of secreted proteins. (c) Suggest why the total in the cell would fall after several hours.
markscheme: (a) Golgi rises from 10% to a peak of 60% at 20 min, then falls to 10% at 120 min (1)
(b) Labelled amino acids enter proteins first at the rough ER (1)
Proteins then move to the Golgi and finally into secretory vesicles (order of peaks) (1)
(c) Vesicles fuse with the plasma membrane and the labelled protein is secreted out of the cell (1)
items.tactic: Unfamiliar context: find the syllabus idea being tested, quote the data (with units) when you describe a trend, then explain it with that idea. One marking point per linked step.
